newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Bloodied Albanian opposition vows new efforts.
newsitem.headline: Bloodied Albanian opposition vows new efforts.

text.p: Albania's opposition, its leaders bloodied or detained in an abortive rally, renewed charges on Saturday that President Sali Berisha was to blame for failed investment schemes but called for talks to resolve turmoil.

The Forum for Democracy, a coalition of 10 disparate political groups, said 15 of its leaders were taken away for a time by police who used truncheons to break up a rally it tried to stage in Tirana's Skanderbeg Square.
"Berisha is at the head of all these pyramids," prominent socialist Kastriot Islami told Reuters, a large purple welt covering one side of his forehead.
"Pyramids in Albania are like Russian dolls (they go on endlessly). If Berisha continues like this he will lose control. The best solution is to discuss the crisis."

It was the second successive weekend that police broke up opposition attempts to stage protests in the capital to blame Berisha's right-wing government for the collapse of pyramid schemes hugely popular in the former Communist country.
But tens of thousands have staged spontaneous protests in the southern port of Vlore this week.

Islami said he had been repeatedly beaten as he approached the square and was thrown into a car, where three plainclothes officers took turns striking him again. He was released from a police station after about two hours.
The Interior Ministry initially denied that any opposition leaders had been detained, saying they had been "summoned" to police stations to be told the rally was illegal.
A second statement said police "took Mr Islami under their protection after he was attacked by some individuals".

Other Forum leaders admitted that police had stalemated their attempts to protest against Berisha using the slogan "flowers instead of stones". They promised to announce new steps in their campaign against the government on Sunday.
"If matters go on like this for much longer, the very existence of Albania as a nation will be in question," Fatos Lubonja, a Forum leader and former political prisoner, told a news conference.
"Instead of engaging in games, Berisha, his executive and the parliament should think about initiating a dialogue on how to find our way out of a situation worsening fast."
The Forum last week turned down Berisha's invitation to cross-party talks, dismissing it as a publicity stunt and demanding the release of comrades detained after violent protests last month.

Its leaders propose forming a "technocrat government" intended to smooth the transition towards market economics. But they say it is up to the government to find the lost life savings of hundreds of thousands of impoverished depositors.
Foreign Minister Tritan Shehu, who also chairs Berisha's right-wing Democratic Party, on Saturday issued a fresh invitation to opposition parties for talks next week.

Opposition leaders said restrictions on the right of assembly made it much more difficult to confront the government than in Bulgaria or Serbia, where mass rallies have secured major concessions from authorities.
"Either it is impossible to hold rallies or secret service men stage provocations," said Islami. "I don't know how many of them there are, maybe 50,000."
